cases.question: Rain keeps hammering the leading edges of our blades, but the blade goes on losing material for days after each downpour has passed — what makes the erosion carry on like that?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: Erosion pits on a wind-turbine blade act as the starting points for further material loss.

cases.note: The wording of the question points most directly at 'Rain that strikes a wind-turbine blade causes the leading edge of that blade to lose material.' — the sentence a reader stops at, and one that is NOT in the necessary set, because the question is not about what starts the loss but about what keeps it going after the rain has stopped. The only sentence in the corpus that says why the damage continues is 'Erosion pits on a wind-turbine blade act as the starting points for further material loss.', and it is reached only indirectly: the question speaks of 'the erosion carry on', while the sentence speaks of erosion pits, starting points and further material loss, none of which the question uses. The set is minimal — the one sentence answers the question alone, and removing it leaves nothing in the corpus that explains continuing loss (the other rain sentences answer what begins the loss, not what sustains it). ANSWERED alone is allowed because the corpus states the fact flatly and there is nothing to hedge about.

cases.question: How can we still measure the condition of a blade's leading edge while the turbine is up and running?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: An ultrasonic sensor measures the thickness of the leading edge of a wind-turbine blade without touching that blade.

alternativeSufficientSets.proposition: A drone that photographs the leading edge of a wind-turbine blade produces images that reveal small erosion pits.
The photographs of a blade inspection reveal an erosion depth of more than two millimetres when the leading edge has lost material.

cases.note: The question is answerable by two independent routes in the corpus, and the case measures whether a system recognises the second one instead of insisting on the first. Route one, the necessary set, is the ultrasonic sensor: it measures the leading-edge thickness without touching the blade, which is the minimal route on its own. Route two is the camera route: a drone photographs the leading edge and the images reveal the small erosion pits, and the photographs of the inspection reveal the erosion depth once the leading edge has lost material — two different sentences, disjoint from route one, that together support the same correct answer about measuring the leading edge in service. B1/B3 are an alternative route rather than corroboration of the ultrasonic sentence: they do not state the ultrasonic fact, they replace it. Both ANSWERED and QUALIFIED are allowed because a correct answer may name one route plainly or name one route and note what it does not establish; either way it must carry a whole route.

cases.question: How does leading-edge erosion end up costing the turbine the power it used to produce?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The severity of an erosion pit depends on its depth and on the width of the material that surrounds it.
The power of a wind-turbine depends on the drag of its blades and on the lift that those blades produce.

cases.corroboration: 'The lift of a wind-turbine blade decreases as the roughness of its leading edge increases.' (wbe-d-aerodynamics.md) — it states the step from the material the leading edge loses to the lift the blade produces, but it mentions neither erosion nor power, so it corroborates the necessary set instead of replacing it.
cases.note: The necessary set has two sentences and no single one of them carries the answer alone. The first (wbe-b-inspection.md) is the corpus's statement of what the erosion takes off the blade: the severity of an erosion pit depends on its depth and on the width of the material that surrounds it, so the pit deepens and the band of material around it narrows — the leading edge of the blade loses material. The second (wbe-d-aerodynamics.md) is the corpus's statement of where the output comes from: the power of a wind-turbine depends on the drag of its blades and on the lift that those blades produce. Drop the first and the answer reaches only the output half of the chain — it would say that the power follows the drag and the lift of the blades, with nothing saying what the erosion does to the leading edge; drop the second and the answer stops at the damage to the leading edge and never reaches the turbine's power. So the two must travel together, and so must the two documents. The corpus offers no single-sentence shortcut: the sentence about the yearly energy production speaks of energy and of roughness, not of erosion and of power, and no sentence outside wbe-d-aerodynamics.md connects the erosion to the output. QUALIFIED is tolerated because the corpus names both the drag and the lift as the sources of the power while the erosion-side sentence speaks only of the material the pits consume, so an answer may state the chain and note that it runs through the lift rather than through the drag.

cases.question: How long will the leading-edge coating last on a turbine that works in sea spray before it has to be renewed?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The service life of a coating depends on the thickness of that coating and on the number of erosion pits that reach it.

cases.note: The corpus carries only the two drivers of a coating's service life — 'The service life of a coating depends on the thickness of that coating and on the number of erosion pits that reach it.' — and no sentence in any of the four files states the service life itself, the rate at which pits reach the coating, or any relation from a thickness to a time in service. The proposition the question needs is therefore a service-life fact that the corpus does not contain, not a paraphrase that has not been found: the workspace cannot carry the whole answer. A correct answer therefore states what the corpus gives and says that the duration itself is not settled (QUALIFIED), or declines to give a duration (ABSTAINED); ANSWERED is not allowed and answerable is false. The sentences about polyurethane and sea spray do not help here, because they concern the erosion rate and not the life of the coating.

cases.question: Our turbines stand at an exposed coastal site and the leading edge of the blade is wearing away fast — does the size of the rain drops matter for how quickly that erosion happens?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The size of the rain drops changes the erosion rate of a wind-turbine blade at an exposed coastal site.
The size of the rain drops does not change the erosion rate of a wind-turbine blade at an exposed coastal site.

cases.contradiction: wbe-a-erosion.md states 'The size of the rain drops changes the erosion rate of a wind-turbine blade at an exposed coastal site.' and wbe-c-coatings.md states 'The size of the rain drops does not change the erosion rate of a wind-turbine blade at an exposed coastal site.' — the same fact, about the same kind of site, with opposite polarity.
cases.note: The corpus holds a literal contradiction here, not merely a tension, so the conflict is not manufactured: the two sentences make the same claim about the same site and one of them is the plain negation of the other. Both are therefore necessary — drop the first and the answer can no longer state the conflict, drop the second and the same — and a correct answer has to carry the conflict: it may report that the corpus says both things, qualify its answer by the conflict, or abstain; what is not correct is an ANSWERED that silently takes one side, because its evidence then carries only half of the necessary set, which is why three dispositions are allowed here. The sentence the wording of the question points most directly at is the general one in wbe-a-erosion.md — 'The erosion rate of a wind-turbine blade depends on the wind speed and on the size of the rain drops that strike it.' — but it settles nothing about the coastal site, so it is neither necessary nor corroborating; no third corpus sentence corroborates the two sides, because the corpus holds no third statement about the rain drops at a coastal site.

cases.question: We fitted a polyurethane coating to the leading edges of the blades that work in sea spray, and the last inspection found a crack in one of them — does that coating still do its job?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A coating of polyurethane reduces the erosion rate of the leading edge of a wind-turbine blade in sea spray.
The erosion rate of a coated blade becomes higher than the rate of an uncoated blade when the coating has a crack.

cases.corroboration: wbe-c-coatings.md's sentence 'A crack in a coating causes sea spray to reach the metal of the wind-turbine blade under that coating.' corroborates the governing sentence by giving the mechanism that turns a cracked coating into a liability.
cases.note: The corpus carries this question's evidence in two forms: the general statement 'A coating of polyurethane reduces the erosion rate of the leading edge of a wind-turbine blade in sea spray.' and a later, narrower statement that corrects it — 'The erosion rate of a coated blade becomes higher than the rate of an uncoated blade when the coating has a crack.' The later sentence governs, because it is the one that applies to the cracked coating the question is about, and the general statement is still needed because the question asks whether the coating is doing its job, which presumes what the coating is for; drop the general statement and the answer says only that a cracked coating is worse than no coating at all, drop the governing sentence and the answer says the coating protects while the corpus says the opposite for the cracked case. The generic protective sentence in wbe-a-erosion.md — 'A protective coating over the leading edge of a wind-turbine blade reduces the erosion rate of that edge.' — is a weaker third version of the general claim and is not needed once the polyurethane sentence is used. ANSWERED and QUALIFIED are both honest here because the condition is part of the answer itself, while a plain abstention is not, since the corpus does settle the case for a cracked coating.

cases.question: The leading edge of one of our blades has gone rough after erosion — how does that affect the lift that blade makes?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: An erosion pit on a wind-turbine blade increases the roughness of that blade and reduces its lift in the same operation.

cases.corroboration: wbe-d-aerodynamics.md's sentence 'The lift of a wind-turbine blade decreases as the roughness of its leading edge increases.' corroborates the lift half of the erosion-pit sentence.
cases.note: The question's terms are shared by two sentences of the same file, wbe-d-aerodynamics.md: 'The lift of a wind-turbine blade decreases as the roughness of its leading edge increases.' and 'An erosion pit on a wind-turbine blade increases the roughness of that blade and reduces its lift in the same operation.' Each takes a different two of the question's terms — roughness, leading edge and lift against erosion pit, roughness and lift — so which of the two the question binds to is decided by the state of the workspace rather than by the wording, which is what makes this a changed binding rather than an ordinary lookup. The necessary evidence is the erosion-pit sentence, because only it carries the link from the pit to the roughness: an answer built on the general law alone would state that a rougher leading edge loses lift but would never say that the pit itself makes the surface rough, which is what the question is about, so the general law is named as corroboration rather than as a second necessary sentence. The corpus holds no third sentence about the lift of an eroded leading edge, so there is nothing else the question could bind to.

cases.question: We had a repair done on the leading edge of a blade that was eroding badly — what actually goes into a repair like that?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A repair of a wind-turbine blade uses a filler material to restore the shape of the leading edge.
A repair of a damaged coating requires the removal of the loose coating and the application of a fresh layer.

cases.corroboration: wbe-d-aerodynamics.md's sentence 'The lift of a repaired wind-turbine blade becomes close to the lift of a new blade when the repair restores the shape of the leading edge.' corroborates the blade-repair reading by stating what restoring the leading-edge shape buys.
cases.note: The corpus uses a repair for two different things and the question does not say which one is meant: 'A repair of a wind-turbine blade uses a filler material to restore the shape of the leading edge.' and 'A repair of a damaged coating requires the removal of the loose coating and the application of a fresh layer.' Both readings sit on the leading edge, since the protective coating is applied over it, so the wording cannot decide between them, and both sentences are necessary: drop the blade sentence and only the coating reading survives, drop the coating sentence and only the blade repair survives. An answer that names one reading and ignores the other has picked a side the corpus does not settle, so the correct answer carries both readings, or qualifies which one it is answering, or asks the asker which repair is meant, which is why all three dispositions are allowed. The sentence in wbe-d-aerodynamics.md about the lift of a repaired blade is named as corroboration because it speaks only to the blade-repair reading and does not resolve the ambiguity.

cases.question: Our cabinet is stocked with the unit doses the wards ask for, and each ward sends us what it needs for the day. Even so, the pharmacy will not release a dose on the strength of that request alone — what has to be on file before a unit dose may be dispensed?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The unit-dose dispensing process of a hospital requires a prescription that names the medicine and its dose.

cases.corroboration: A3 corroborates the necessary set: “A barcode on a unit dose of a medicine allows the cabinet to check that medicine against the prescription of the ward.” — the check the cabinet performs presupposes exactly the prescription that the necessary sentence makes a requirement.
cases.note: LOWER_RANKED_NECESSARY: the wording deliberately repeats the vocabulary of the most direct match — “A dispensing cabinet in a hospital pharmacy stores the unit doses of the medicines that the ward asks for.” — so a reader who stops at that sentence concludes that the ward's request is what the pharmacy works from and never reaches the sentence that actually answers the question. The necessary sentence, “The unit-dose dispensing process of a hospital requires a prescription that names the medicine and its dose.”, is reached only indirectly: the argument that a request is not enough has to be turned into “what does the process require”, and the corpus answers that in other words (“requires”, “prescription that names the medicine and its dose”). The direct match is not needed: it says only what the cabinet stores, not what the process requires, so the necessary set is the single sentence and stays minimal.

cases.question: After a patient is admitted, our ward hands out medicines at every dosing round. Which document is the authority on what that patient should be getting, and what has that document got to contain?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The record of an admission contains the list of medicines that the ward gives to the patient.
The list of medicines at the admission of a patient acts as the reference for every dose that the ward gives later.

cases.corroboration: C5 corroborates the necessary set: “The reconciliation of an admission in a hospital pharmacy reduces the number of medicines that the ward gives without a record.” — it ties the admission record and the list in it to the medicines the ward actually gives.
cases.note: JOINTLY_NECESSARY: both sentences are needed and neither carries the answer alone. “The record of an admission contains the list of medicines that the ward gives to the patient.” says which document holds the list and what the list is, but says nothing about the list governing the doses the ward gives later. “The list of medicines at the admission of a patient acts as the reference for every dose that the ward gives later.” says the list at the admission is the reference for every later dose, but names no document and does not say where the list is recorded. Drop the first and “which document” is unanswered; drop the second and “what governs the doses afterwards” is unanswered. The two sentences come from one file but contribute different halves of the answer, and neither of them is a necessary sentence of another slice of this assignment.

cases.question: A unit dose is sitting in the cabinet with a label that the label printer produced wrong. What has to happen to that dose before it is allowed to go out to the ward?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A unit dose with a label that the printer produced incorrectly requires a manual check before the ward receives it.

alternativeSufficientSets.proposition: A label that the printer produced incorrectly requires the pharmacist to check it against the prescription.

cases.note: ALTERNATIVE_SUFFICIENT: two routes to the same correct answer, in two different documents. The necessary set is “A unit dose with a label that the printer produced incorrectly requires a manual check before the ward receives it.”, because the question asks about a unit dose in the cabinet and about the moment before the ward receives it, and that sentence says both. The alternative sufficient set is the single sentence “A label that the printer produced incorrectly requires the pharmacist to check it against the prescription.”, which reaches the same correct answer from the labelling document and adds who checks the label and against what. A correct answer may stand on either set; neither of the two sentences is a necessary sentence of another slice of this assignment.

cases.question: How long does the verification of a single unit dose take at our cabinet, from the moment the technician lifts the dose off the shelf to the moment the ward receives it?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The reading of a barcode takes a fraction of a second on a scanner that sits beside the cabinet.

cases.corroboration: A5 corroborates the necessary set: “A picking machine in a hospital pharmacy takes the unit dose from the cabinet and records that removal in the log.” — the chain between the shelf and the ward has more than one step, so the barcode read cannot be the whole of the time asked about.
cases.note: MISSING_PREREQUISITE: the corpus carries exactly one duration, “The reading of a barcode takes a fraction of a second on a scanner that sits beside the cabinet.”, and that single sentence is the necessary set, because it is the only timing fact an answer may stand on. The end-to-end time the question asks for needs propositions the corpus does not contain: how long the comparison against the ward's prescription takes, how long the manual check on a mismatch takes, what the ward's own check of the label costs in time, and how those steps compose into a cycle time. The workspace therefore cannot carry the whole answer, and the honest dispositions are QUALIFIED (give the barcode read time and say the rest is not in the workspace) and ABSTAINED. The question also has a second reading that the corpus does support — the time of the barcode read alone — so this case carries an ambiguity shape as well; if the milestone wants the AMBIGUITY slot for A3, it can be re-filed as such with answerable set to true, and the evidence and dispositions would not change.

cases.question: We want the cabinet to check every unit dose against the ward's prescription. Can it confirm the strength of the medicine from the barcode on the dose alone?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The barcode of a medicine provides the identifier of the product and the strength of that medicine.
The barcode of a unit dose provides the batch number of that dose but not the strength of the medicine in it.

cases.corroboration: hpd-b-identification.md also states: 'A mismatch between the strength on a barcode and the strength in a prescription requires a manual check.' That sentence corroborates the identification side of the conflict - it shows the workflow expects the strength to be readable from the barcode - and it is not part of the necessary set.
cases.contradiction: hpd-b-identification.md states 'The barcode of a medicine provides the identifier of the product and the strength of that medicine.' and hpd-c-reconciliation.md states 'The barcode of a unit dose provides the batch number of that dose but not the strength of the medicine in it.' The two sentences conflict about the same thing - whether the barcode of the dispensed medicine carries its strength - and the corpus nowhere distinguishes a medicine-level barcode from a unit-dose barcode, so the conflict stands unresolved on the corpus's own terms.
cases.note: Both sentences are necessary and neither carries the conflict alone: the identification document says the barcode of the medicine carries its strength, the reconciliation document says the barcode of the unit dose carries the batch number and not the strength. An answer that quotes only one of them has silently picked a side, which is exactly what this condition forbids; the corpus nowhere states that a medicine's barcode and a unit dose's barcode are two different objects, so the conflict cannot be closed from the corpus and a correct answer has to carry it or to abstain. ANSWERED is not allowed here because a flat statement of one side - or even of both sides without saying that they conflict - reads as a settled answer, which this condition forbids. The strength-mismatch sentence of the identification document and the cabinet-checks-the-barcode sentence of the dispensing document are background a reader may add, but neither is needed to carry the conflict, so the necessary set is the two conflicting sentences and nothing else.

cases.question: Does anything in the dispensing workflow check a unit dose's expiry date before that dose leaves the cabinet?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A picking machine in a hospital pharmacy takes the unit dose from the cabinet and records that removal in the log.

cases.note: The corpus says nothing about expiry: no sentence of the four hpd documents mentions a date, a shelf life, an expiry or a dose that has gone off, so the subject of the question is genuinely outside what the corpus holds and the only honest disposition is ABSTAINED. The one sentence listed is the nearest thing the corpus does hold about the picking step, and it is listed precisely because it makes the gap visible: 'A picking machine in a hospital pharmacy takes the unit dose from the cabinet and records that removal in the log.' It fixes what the corpus says happens when a dose leaves the cabinet, and leaves the expiry question with no answer at all - the corpus does not contain the answer, and no sentence of it would let a reader infer one.

cases.question: Our labels print the preparation and the amount it carries, yet staff still pick the wrong dose off the shelf. Under what condition does the wording on a label actually become ambiguous?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The wording of a label becomes ambiguous when the amount is not printed next to its name.

cases.note: The question's evidence exists in the corpus in two forms and the later one governs. The earlier form is the flat claim 'A printed label states the preparation and the amount that the preparation carries.' The later sentence of the same file qualifies it: 'The wording of a label becomes ambiguous when the amount is not printed next to its name.' That later sentence is the one that governs, and it alone answers the question. An answer that rests only on that earlier general claim would not answer the question at all and would drop the condition the corpus attaches to the label, so the necessary set is the single governing sentence. The earlier statement is deliberately not in the necessary set: the question already puts that general claim in its premise, so it is not evidence for the answer. QUALIFIED is allowed alongside ANSWERED because an honest answer may also say that the corpus's later sentence narrows its earlier, more general statement, and that is a stated limit rather than a different answer.

cases.question: The ward has taken the dose from the pharmacy cabinet. Before it reaches the patient, does anybody still check the dose itself?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A unit dose in a hospital pharmacy has a label that the ward checks before the dose reaches the patient.

cases.note: The question's terms bind to more than one sentence of one file. The necessary sentence is 'A unit dose in a hospital pharmacy has a label that the ward checks before the dose reaches the patient.' The competing sentence sits in the same file, hpd-a-dispensing.md: 'A unit dose that does not match the barcode of its medicine requires a manual check before the ward receives it.' Both are about a check on a unit dose around the handover to the ward and they share the terms unit dose, check and ward, so the wording of the question cannot separate them; only the moment does - before the ward has the dose at all, against before the patient gets it. Which of the two the question binds to therefore depends on the state of the workspace, that is on which of the two sentences the workspace holds and surfaces, and not on the wording alone. The barcode sentence does not answer this question, because its check happens before the ward has the dose and so is not a check on the dose after receipt; only the ward's own check of the label before the dose reaches the patient answers it, which is why the necessary set holds that one sentence alone. QUALIFIED is allowed alongside ANSWERED because an honest answer may add that the pharmacy-side check happens earlier in the chain, which is a stated limit and not a different answer.

cases.question: On the north turbine nothing can reach the blade - no crane to lift it, no drone to fly over it - and we still have to say how much of the leading edge is gone; how is that number obtained?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: The photographs of a blade inspection reveal an erosion depth of more than two millimetres when the leading edge has lost material.

cases.note: The wording of the question points most directly at the sentences of the inspection file that describe how a reading is taken on a blade that nobody can reach - the ultrasonic sentence that reads the thickness of the edge without any contact, and the drone sentence, whose images show only small pits - because the scene stresses that nothing can reach the blade and the last clause of the question asks how the number is obtained, which is a question about method. Neither of those sentences is in the necessary set: the drone is excluded by the wording of the question itself, and the ultrasonic reading answers how a reading is taken but not how much material the leading edge has lost. The necessary sentence is reached only indirectly, through the question's demand for an amount rather than for a method: the corpus states how much of a leading edge is gone in a consequence clause, not in a method sentence - the photographs of a blade inspection reveal an erosion depth of more than two millimetres when the leading edge has lost material. That sentence is necessary because the question asks how much of the leading edge is gone, and this is the one place where the corpus gives an amount of lost leading edge; the photographs it speaks of are the photographs of an inspection, not of a drone, so the scene of the question does not exclude them, and what they reveal is the depth that has to be reported. Drop it and an answer can still name a way of measuring the edge, but it never says how much is gone, so the answer either stops at the method and does not answer the question or collapses into 'the corpus does not say', and that is not one of the allowed dispositions of this case. The necessary sentence is minimal - one sentence carries the whole figure - and a reader who stopped at the most direct match would answer with a method and would miss the necessary evidence entirely.

cases.question: We are buying a leading-edge protection system for a new turbine; when does the coating have to go on, and what decides what we pay for it?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A leading-edge protection system on a wind-turbine blade requires an application of the coating before the blade leaves the factory.
The cost of a coating system for a wind-turbine blade depends on the size of the blade and on the number of leading edges that need protection.

cases.note: The question has two halves and each half of the answer is carried by exactly one corpus sentence, so neither sentence carries the answer alone. The first half - when the protection is applied - is carried by the sentence saying a leading-edge protection system requires an application of the coating before the blade leaves the factory, and the second half - what drives the price - is carried by the sentence saying the cost of a coating system depends on the size of the blade and on the number of leading edges that need protection. Drop the first and the answer never says that the coating is a factory step; drop the second and it never says what the price follows from. No other sentence of the corpus touches either half, which is why the set has no alternative route.

cases.question: Our offshore turbine has been running in sea spray for most of the year; is the scheduled inspection enough, or does it need another one?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A second inspection of a wind-turbine blade becomes necessary after a period of operation in sea spray.

alternativeSufficientSets.proposition: Sea spray causes a higher erosion rate on a wind-turbine blade than dry air produces.
The inspection interval for a wind-turbine blade in a coastal site depends on the erosion rate that the site produces.

cases.note: The necessary sentence states the conclusion outright - a second inspection becomes necessary after a period of operation in sea spray - and it is minimal, because removing it leaves nothing in the corpus that says an inspection recurs. A different route to the same correct answer exists and is named here: the pair about sea spray producing a higher erosion rate than dry air, together with the sentence saying the inspection interval at a coastal site depends on the erosion rate that the site produces - two sentences from another file, which reach the same conclusion by the chain sea spray raises the rate, the coastal interval follows the rate, so the next inspection falls sooner. The alternative set shares no sentence with the necessary set, so the question is answerable from the corpus in two distinct ways.

cases.question: One of our offshore blades came back from the yard with its polyurethane coating opened up along the leading edge; on that blade, can the sea spray still get at the metal underneath?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A crack in a coating causes sea spray to reach the metal of the wind-turbine blade under that coating.

cases.note: The terms of the question - the polyurethane coating, the sea spray, the metal under the coating, the blade - are shared by two sentences of the same file, and which of the two the answer has to stand on is settled by the state of the workspace, not by the wording. With a sound coating the binding is the sentence saying that a coating of polyurethane reduces the erosion rate of the leading edge in sea spray; in the state this case describes, the coating has opened up along the edge, so the binding is the necessary sentence, which says that a crack in a coating causes sea spray to reach the metal of the blade under it. The necessary sentence is minimal - one sentence carries the whole answer to the question - and a reader who bound the sound-coating sentence without looking at the state of that blade would answer that the spray is turned back, which is wrong for this state. The question says 'opened up' rather than the corpus word for the damage, so the binding decision follows from the state of the blade rather than from a wording cue.

cases.question: The pharmacy keeps a log of what leaves the cabinets, and the manager keeps saying it is more than paperwork. What can the pharmacy no longer tell you about its own stock if a dose comes out and the log never mentions it?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: An unrecorded unit dose in a hospital pharmacy reduces the ability of the pharmacy to account for the medicines in its cabinets.

cases.note: The question asks what is LOST, and the wording it uses lands first on the two log sentences of hpd-a-dispensing.md: 'A picking machine in a hospital pharmacy takes the unit dose from the cabinet and records that removal in the log.' and 'The dispensing log of a hospital pharmacy provides the record of every unit dose that left the cabinet.' Both are about the record itself and neither states a consequence, so a reader who stopped at the most direct lexical match would answer 'the pharmacy has a log of every dose that left the cabinet' and never say what the log is worth. The necessary sentence is reached only indirectly, by a paraphrase of 'what can the pharmacy no longer tell you about its own stock' as 'reduces the ability of the pharmacy to account for the medicines in its cabinets'. Remove it and the answer says nothing about the loss, so the set of one is minimal and necessary.

cases.question: A patient is admitted with a medicine of their own that the ward does not stock. What does the pharmacy have to put in the record of the admission, and what happens to the patient if that never gets done?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A medicine that the patient brought in and that the ward does not hold requires a note in the record of the admission.
A missing entry in the record of an admission creates a risk of a duplicate dose.

cases.note: Neither sentence carries the answer alone, and each contributes something the other does not. The first is the only statement of the duty itself: a medicine the patient brought in that the ward does not hold requires a note in the record of the admission; without it the answer names a risk but not the act that the pharmacy owes. The second is the only statement of what the risk is: a missing entry in that record creates a risk of a duplicate dose; without it the answer states a piece of paperwork but leaves the patient harm unexplained, and the question's second half unanswered. The corpus holds no single sentence that carries both the duty and the consequence, and the two are not redundant with one another, so the two-sentence set is the minimal necessary one.

cases.question: Two of the ward's preparations have names that are almost identical and the staff keep picking up the wrong one. What on the packaging is meant to stop that?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: Two preparations with close names need a distinct label on every wrapper.

alternativeSufficientSets.proposition: The colour of a wrapper lets the staff separate one preparation from another.

cases.corroboration: hpd-d-labelling.md: 'The colour of a wrapper lets the staff separate one preparation from another.' states the packaging feature from the staff's side and corroborates the necessary set on its own.
cases.note: The answer is the packaging: the wrapper has to make the two preparations tellable apart. Two different sentences carry it, and a correct answer may rest on either. The necessary set I designate is the labelling file's sentence about close names, which states the requirement itself — a distinct label on every wrapper. The alternative sufficient set is the colour sentence, which supports the same answer from the ward's side — the colour of a wrapper lets the staff separate one preparation from another — and therefore carries a correct answer without the designated sentence. The milestone should score an answer resting on either route as carrying the answer; I designate the first because it states what the pharmacy must do, while the second states how the separation works in the ward's hands.

cases.question: The scanner beside the cabinet could not read the barcode on one pack this morning. What happens to that dose?

necessaryEvidence.proposition: A scanner that cannot read the barcode of a medicine requires the cabinet to stop and to ask the pharmacist.

cases.note: The question's terms are shared with another sentence of the same file, and the wording alone does not separate the two. 'A scanner that cannot read the barcode of a medicine requires the cabinet to stop and to ask the pharmacist.' and 'A medicine with two similar packages requires a check of the barcode before the unit dose leaves the cabinet.' both turn on the barcode, on the cabinet and on the dose that is about to leave it, and the question's wording — the scanner beside the cabinet, the barcode, the dose — matches both. What separates them is the state of the workspace: here the scanner could not read the code, so the unreadable-barcode rule governs and the cabinet must stop and ask the pharmacist, while the look-alike-package rule is the one that is not reached. A reader who matched on the shared vocabulary of barcode, cabinet and dose alone would land on the second sentence and answer that the barcode must be checked, which does not say what happens to a dose whose code cannot be read. The necessary set is the single sentence of the unreadable-barcode rule; it is minimal, because no other sentence of the corpus says what a failing scanner obliges the cabinet to do.
